Those notices are only to be -sent to the men who have been already examined and found in Category A. It was not the desire to call back the men already examined and -found in a lower category. The idea was not, if possible, to have these men come up for rehearing. We are anxious to get only the men who are medically fit. On section 1-Quebec notarial copies to foe deemed originals; mortgage to include hypothec:

I notice that the Bill says that a duly certified notarial copy of any instrument executed in the province of Quebec " and- preserved in the records of a notary public " shall foe deemed to be an original document. When a notary dies his records are in the keeping of another notary or at a prothonotary's office. Perhaps it might be well to say " and preserved in the the records of a notary public of the province of Quebec, whether at his office, or at the court." There is a possibility that has not been provided for. In the event of the death of a notary in our province his records are no longer kept at his office, or at his successor's office, but are transferred to the prothonotary's office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I recognize the possibility of that happening, but it is not clear to me that the wording would not cover it. At all events there is no objection to making it absolutely clear. I think it would meet the hon. gentleman's suggestion if we amended the section. I therefore move that:
That section 1, subsection' 69M, be amended by striking out the word "notarial" in the first line thereof and by adding after the word "Quebec" in the fourth line of the said sub-section, the following words "or in the office of the prothonotary of the Superior Court in any district of the said province".
Would that meet it?
Yes.
Is that the only place where they would be deposited?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the only place where they would be deposited that I am aware of. There are provisions for what happens if they are absolutely destroyed. Then it would be a question of using a copy from the registrar. But I do not think that we need look forward to that. That is the only place I know of and I think the honourable gentleman would agree that where it was an original document it would be kept on record. But, inasmuch as we are providing for a case where certification would be by the prothonotary and not by the notary, it might perhaps be well to omit the word " notarial " before the word " copy " so that it would read:
A duly certified copy of any deed, mortgage, hypothec or other authentic instrument executed
in the province of Quebec and preserved in the records of a notary public or . in the office of the prothonotary-
Because there could otherwise be no daily certified copy unless it was certified by the notary. We would have to provide for certification by the prothonotary.

A duly certified notarial copy of any deed, mortgage, hypothec or other authentic instrument executed in the province of Quebec.

I want to make an explanation as to how these grades have been arrived at. There have been, as I have said, no legal grades in the western provinces, including British Columbia, but since 1905 there has been more or less agitation to have grades established and inspectors made available, so that if people wished to purchase and sell upon grade there should be the legal grade, and inspection provided therefor. These grades were arrived at in this way: First by correspondence by the department with people interested in the West. After that had been carried on for several years and more or less information had been gathered, an officer of my department made a tour through the West, going as far as British Columbia, and took up the matter with the Department of Agriculture in each province. Information was thus gained personally, and an opportunity afforded the officer of the department to discuss the matter with those who probably understood most about it in these different provinces. Communications were also had with boards of trade, with people in the hay trade, and so on. To make a long story short, the grades established by the Bill have been agreed upon and approved by all the provinces through their Departments of ' Agriculture. The point under discussion is a very nice one. I have always admired the certainty and authoritative style of the minister (Sir George Foster). I would like to remind him, now that he is sitting between two very eminent lawyers, that he is dealing with a very intricate question of law. There is just one fallacy in his whole argument and that is that a man who' sells any article, particularly an article of food for man or beast, contracts to sell a merchantable article. It will not do for him to sell, for instance, butter, looking nice on the outside, in a regulation keg or box, of the proper weight, colour, taste and everything all right as far as the eye can see, although that tub of butter is not merchantable. It is a common-law principle that the man who sells that tub of butter undertakes that he is selling a merchantable commodity fit for the 'purpose for which he is selling it. If the man's name is on the tub and it turns out that the butter is not merchantable, although it looks all right, or if it turns out not to have been put up in such a way ,as to stand the journey for which it was intended, not properly salted, or not properly coopered, there is recourse against him. What the hon. 'gentleman (Sitting around me want is that the man who sells a tub of butter shall put his name on it so that he may be held responsible. Before going into Committee of Supply, I wish to call the attention of the House to a very urgent matter touching the safety of the public, and the avoidance of disaster through the explosion of munitions. On February 5 I wrote the fol'owing letter to the Minister of Militia: Dear Sir, '

One of these fires was only stopped at about five feet from a large mass of t.n.t., another one caused an explosion a few days ago, which will probably result in deaitlh of two men.

What is the present state of this work, and when may we expect to be reinstated in the new building?

A week ago I invited the members of the House to visit and inspect these works, and I am very glad that a great many availed themselves of the opportunity and are thereby as familiar with the real state of the work as I am. Generally speaking, the structure of the building is about completed, excepting the main tower and six smaller towers, the steel of which has already been erected. The remainder of the work yet to be done is in the nature of finishing'up. The plan of the new building is very different from the old. Along the front, from the outside, it looks about the same, but that is the only respect in which the plan is the same as that of the old building. I had hoped up to the last month or two that it would he possible to have the building completed so that it would be ready for occupation during the next session of Parliament, but I am afraid that that will be a physical impossibility. Two buildings, practically complete in themselves, occupy the sites of the old HouSe of Commons and Senate chambers; these, for purposes of designation, are called office blocks. They com-prise'most of the three upper storeys of the building, the remaining part of that space consisting of rooms for committees and other general purposes. These office blocks are lighted on both sides from very wide wells, and will embrace, I think, eighty-four offices, each about ten by twenty feet. We anticipate that these will be completed by 1st November, and while it may seem like sacrilege, I confess that we intend to occupy this part of the building, when it is completed, by such members of the Civil Service as can be put- in them. This course is being taken because the amount which we are paying for rent in Ottatva is simply terrible, and it is only good business to utilize every foot of space that is at all available. The building is being constructed by a committee, of which I happen to be chairman, by virtue of my office. All purchases are being made by tender and contract.
Who are the other members of the committee?

From the Senate: Sir James Lougheed, Hon. Robert Watson and

Hon. G. D. Robertson; from the Commons: Hon. Mr. Ballantyne, Dr. Reid, Mr. Calder and myself. I think that is all. The system followed is practically this: A board consisting of the two architects and the deputy minister meets from time to time and decides upon what is required in the immediate future.
It then makes a recommendation to the Parliamentary Committee, asking the right to call for tenders. Advertisements calling for tenders are inserted in a number of the leading newspapers, wherever it is thought it will be necessary, and when the tenders are opened they .are examined by the technical officers. A report is made to the committee, and the committee decide upon the letting of the contracts. Contracts have recently been let for the heating, the plumbing, the ventilation, the heating plant, the wiring, and the conduits. What I call the heating plant is the boilers and automatic stokers. Tenders have been called for for steel casements for the windows. That matter has not been finally decided. Tenders have also been opened for the furnishing of panel boards^ switch boards, transformers and electrical supplies. Those have not yet been decided. I can only assure the House that every dollar that is being expended in that building is passing under the strictest scrutiny of the Parliamentary Committee, and the lowest tender is in every ca-se being accepted, unless the very strongest reason can be given to the contrary. We have not accepted the lowest tender in every case, but if we have not, it is because there were reasons so potent that the ordinary man would not haye accepted the lowest tender. The amount spent up to date would be in the vicinity of $3,000,000, or perhaps a little less; it was1 $2,700,000 some two or three months ago. It would be. pretty hard to form an estimate of what it will take to finish the building, but it will run to at least $5,000,000, and possibly a little more, depending to some extent upon, the character of the inside decorations. The House, I think, will agree with me that if we are going to finish,the building we should finish it properly. If we come to the conclusion that, on. account of the financial situation, we cannot put in the proper decorations*, we should not put in decorations at all. It is the intention to finish the building as expeditiously as possible, making it more than a building for commercial purposes, a building that to some extent will be suitable for the capital of the Dominion of Canada. Some portions of it may be con-

sidered- as -a work of art. The public, will agree, I am sure, if we are erecting new parliament buildings- for the Dominion of Canada, we should build practically the latest thing in the -architectural world today.

What system of heating has been decided upon? I ask this because, prior to the beginning of the work, in fact, before the selection of a committee to superintend the work,. I wrote the then Minister of Public Works, suggesting that there be employed a certain modern method of heating which wouid do away with boilers and all that kind of thing in the building itself. The reply I received indicated that some such idea as that would be adopted. Later on I saw it was proposed to heat the building by electricity, but, judging by what my hon. friend has said- to-night, that scheme has not been carried out.

As regards electricity,
this is the first intimation I have received that such a method of heating was in contemplation. We would have to have another water-power practically equal to the Chaudiere, in order properly to heat this building by electricity. Somebody has to devise a new scheme of electrical heating before it will be commercially feasible for a building of that kind. The contracts have all been- let for the heating plant, which consists of a central plant on Cliff street, down from the Hill, near the old Supieme Court building. The plan provides for six large boilers with automatic stokers. It is to be a hot-water heating system. I am speaking now without any actual knowledge, but I think I am right in stating that the scheme is to send the steam up the hill in large pipes, this steam to be used1 to heat water in the building for circulation throughout the building. That is, we transmit the steam from the central heating plant to the building rather than transmit the hot water. It is a technical matter on which I am not in a position to pass judgment.
It is a hot water system.

Yes, but the hot water is heated by steam generated in the central plant. This plant will be of sufficient capacity to take care of the heating in the East Block, the West Block, the Lange-vin Block, the post office block and the Supreme Court buildings. As the system is on a unit basis, it might possibly be extended.

What has been decided with regard to the main tower? There appears to be provision made for a portion of it, but, though that has stood there for a length of time, yet either for reasons of convenience in connection with the rest of the work or because the plan has not been finally adopted, the work has not been gone on with.

That is largely because
the architect has, as he says, -been dreaming over it. There is no reason why he should not keep on dreaming for a few months longer. Naturally, and I think quite rightly, he wishes- to have, from an architectural point of view in connection with the rest of the building, the best tower he can devise. The main tower will be built in front of the building as now erected, and it is to be 44 -feet square- at the base, running up that -size perhaps 150 -feet. I am speaking now offhand. It then tapers off to some extent. I am- not architect enough to describe to my hon. friend all the beauties of this tower, but when completed it will be 260 feet from the ground level. The foundation will undoubtedly be laid this year and possibly some portion of the substructure, but I d-o not think it is the intention to complete the tower until another year. It is not a necessary -portion of the building. There is, in my judgment, no reason to spending the money involved, a fairly large amount, until we have to spend it. The building could be completed and occupied without the construction of this tower, although it is- the intention to proceed with it and complete it in the ordinary course of affars.
I understood the minister to say that -by next November it would be possible to occupy a number of rooms in the new building for office purposes.
Eighty-four rooms.

The minister justifies
that on the ground of saving rent?
Yes.

Might it not be possible to do something of the same kind in connection with the chambers of the House of Commons and the Senate-not- that it would result in a saving of rent, but it would result in Parliament meeting, eo to speak, in ite own building again. My hon. friend mentioned that the question of decorations had not been actually decided upon. I understood him to say that matter was still o-pen, and he added that if the decora-

tione were to be gone on with, it was desirable that they should be excellent in every respect, and, in fact, the very best that can be found in the Dominion. With that I entirely agree, but the two chambers might be sufficiently advanced for the purposes of occupation, and the decorations could go on in the recesses ibetween sessions. I merely offer that as a suggestion to the minister.

I have a great deal of sympathy with suggestions offered by my hon. friend, and I can assure him that meets with a great deal of favour foy different members of the Government.
Of course, we .are, in the judgment of the House, very largely in connection with this national building. The only difficulty is that the contractors and architects say it is impossible; I do. not mean impossible in the sense that it could not possibly be done, but practically, they say, it is impossible, and I would not want to urge my views against the professional views of such men as the contractors and architects of this building.
Impossible to have it ready for next session?

Practically impossible. I pressed it upon them very strongly-in fact,
I commenced pressing it over three months ago and other members of the Government have also pressed it, but the architects are very strongly of the opinion that it would be a very great mistake. Eighty-four rooms *could be finished, and I think that would be quite sufficient for the use of members of the Government and hon.. gentlemen, but the difficulty is there will be practically no offices ready for the officers of the House, and as my hon. friend knows, it takes a very large amount of space to take care of the requirements of the officers of the two Houses of Parliament. I am rather forced to the conclusion that it would be almost an impossible task to have the building reasonably ready for the next session of Parliament.
I trust that in the tower which the minister has described proper provision will be made for the lodgment of such state .prisoners as we may have to take care of from time to time.
It is my intention to fix up a room in the basement of the tower for such characters as my hon. friend has described.
That is absolutely unconstitutional. The proper place to put state prisoners is in the tower.
If I remember correctly, the work was to be done by force contract. Does that apply to the whole building?
That included the whole building from the basement to the top of the tower, everything on the outside and everything on the inside.
Would the contractors get a certain percentage on such work as the heating?
It covers everything one could imagine that goes into the construction of the building. [DOT]
Is hot-water heating a good system?

The hot-water heating system passed the experimental stage years ago, and it is to be found in the large buildings and hospitals and universities in Toronto and Montreal and practically every American city. There is no question whatever about its economy and its usefulness.
I cannot give my hon. friend exact figures as to what the architects think will he saved, but there will be a very great saving of fuel and in cost, and it will do away with all dust and soot. There is just as much difference as between the steam car and the electric street car. Every one knows that in a building heated by an internal plant there is a large amount of dust accumulating all the time, and this will be absolutely eliminated in the new building. From the standpoint of cleanliness .and economy I think there is no question whatever as to the advisability of a central heating plant.

I was not thinking so
much of the isolation of the plant as of the merits, of the hot-water heating system.

I do not know enough about the technical side of it to answer my hon. friend, but we all know that all over this country buildings are heated by steam or by hot water. Generally speaking, I think the hot-water system is not used in very high buildings. This question has been gone into very thoroughly by the technical officers, and they have decided on the hot-water system as being the best and most economical method of heating.

What percentage is paid to the contractor under this force agreement over and above cost?	*

Mr. 'CAiRVELL: I have not the contract with me, but from my recollection they get eight per cent up to $4,000,000, seven per cent for the next million, and I think there is no commission after $5,000,000.

I regret to say, there are none.	[DOT]

I do not think that the . present contractors, eminent as they are in their own line, occupy any particular place in the artistic world in Canada, and I think my hon. friend will be well advised to terminate the contract as soon as he reasonably can, and I would suggest that the. decorations be made under some other arrangement. No.

And therefore he wou'd be in a much better position to speak of the exact terms and conditions than I would be. But whether my memory is correct or not, I think I am safe in saying, from what the building has cost up to the present time and from the contracts that have already been entered into, that the building will cost $5,000,000 exclusive of decorations, and as the percentage stops at $5,000,000, the point of my hon. friend is therefore not so very important. Suppose the actual construction cost was $4,500,000, that would leave a margin of $500,000, and if that is to he used for decorations, I submit that
it should not form part of the original contract. My hon. friend will remember that my name did appear on the committee, but I never acted, for reasons which it is not necessary to go into now.
The word "decorations" covers a very broad field.	-
You will make it an Clastic term.

It covers a very great
part of the building. For instance, I would include in the word "decorations'" the marble arches, whether the entrance be finished in an elaborate manner or not. If you finish that hall in marble, as I think a large part of it should be finished, that work must be done by just such men ,as the present contractors. If, on the other band, we are to have a plain wall covered with valuable paintings, I think my hon. friend's criticism would be very much to the point, hut I can assure him that it is not intended to finish this in .painting, but in something very much more substantial, and I am satisfied that $5,000,000 will have been expended long before we come 'to the time of paintings ,and such artistic decorations as will he covered by that term.

I was appointed a member of that committee two years ago, and, like my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy), I resigned, after having attended the preliminary meetings of the committee, not that I found much to be criticised up to the time of my resignation, hut when I resigned I found we were overstepping the mark. The Parliament of Canada had voted a certain sum. toward the restoration of the buildings as they were before the fire, hut then it was decided to raze what was * left of the buildings and to erect a new Parliament building. I thought I had not been appointed a member of that committee to erect a new building, hut to restore the old. Be that as it may, the construction has gone on, and I must say that I have no fault to find, from an architectural point of view especially. I think this new building will be a monument worthy of Canada. 1 quite agree with my hon. friend from Russell when, he says it is quite a different thing to complete the artistic part of that building and the purely structural part of it. I believe that Peter Lyall and Company are a very reliable firm, and with regard to the erection of the structure itself, I think they stand well as the head of their profession in Canada. But with regard to the artistic

end of this monumental building, I say that the suggestion of the hon. gentleman from Russell should 'be accepted. The Parliament of Canada, comprising the -House of Commons and Senate, is not an ordinary building. It is a national temple, so to speak, .and will last for generations and generations. It has been my privilege to travel twice around the world, and I have seen many parliaments, and I may say that all parliaments are profusely artistic in their completion. We need not go ibeyond Canada. The Parliament buildings in Quebec are really a gem; but to -proceed from one country to another, the Capitol in Washington, the House of Commons in England, the Palais Bourbon in France, and the new Parliament buildings in South Africa, are some of the most artistic buildings in the world. It seems to me that the young artists of Canada should contribute towards the completion of the interior of the building, and that we should imitate what has been done at Westminster, England, where you read on the walls of Parliament the whole history of the English people and of the English nation. You have there splendid paintings, and sculptures which are masterpieces. You have the same class of works in Washington and in Paris. We have a history behind us in Canada, and we have a -great future ahead of us, and if a oonoours were established, it seem-s to me we would have something to stimulate the genius of our young artists, and at the same time to commemorate. the salient facts and great periods in the history of Canada. It is not necessary that this commemoration, in vieiw of the present financial crisis, -should materialize at once, but plans can ibe laid out f-or the future, as a conco-urs of that nature always takes -months andi years before being realized. I am just throwing out the idea.

I do not think there is any question whatever that my hon. friend is right. I have not read over the contract, but it would take a great deal of argument to make me believe that the Parliament of Canada appointed -a committee to purchase valuable paintings. As I view it, we are to erect buildings, and it may be a hundred years before the decorations are finished.
We can not wait that long.

No, perhaps we cannot wait. I do not think there will be any intention on the part of any one to pay a commission to the present contractors for supplying -paintings in the future. I think

my hon. friends can rest assured as to that At any rate, if I occupy -my present position for a few years, hon. gentlemen can rest assured that we will erect the building, and let -posterity take care of the artistic side of it.

When this contract or agreement was entered into, I understood the intention was to repair the old building. We all know that the architects reported upon the walls of the old buildings shortly after the disastrous fire, and stated that very large portions of them were good, and all that they could be repaired and built upon. After the information I received at that time, like many other, I was quite surprised on returning to Ottawa during the summer to find that the buildings had been absolutely razed, andi that a new building was being constructed. I am not saying a word of criticism of the hon. minister in reference to the action he has taken, because this arrangement, I understand, was made by a committee of which my hon. friend was not at that time a member,- and the agreement was entered into for the purpose of rebuilding the structure on what is known as a force contract. The builders were to receive 8 per cent profit on the cost of the work up to $4,000,000; and on the cost from $4,000,000 to $5,000,000 they were to receive a profit of 7 per cent. I understand that somewhere in the vicinity of $3,000,000 has been expended?
Yes, in that vicinity

That being so, the contractors have m-ade a very handsome thing in the past year on this work. My hon. friend says there is an agreement in regard to- th-is matter. In the present condition of business in this- country it might be decided that a contract might be changed or varied to a certain extent and an opportunity given to others without giving too much profit to any individual. I have nothing to say against the contractors; they are men who have been in this business for years and as far as I know they have a splendid reputation for doing work of this character. There may be an argument that it would be better to -construct certain public works under force contract rather than under the regular contracting system. That might have been so if the original intention had been followed of repairing the building, for changes might be found necessary in the course of the work and these could be more readily made under a force contract. But it is only up to a certain point, possibly in the construction of the stone work and the steel

structure, that the work should' be conducted in this particular way. When the committee asked for tenders for putt-ins? in the heating system, -the ventilating system, the sanitary arrangements and the elevators, for which I understand contracts are -let, there ie no good reason why others outside of the contractors for these different classes of work should be given a percentage or a rake-off, in view of the fact that they have nothing whatever to do with the work. When the committee make a contract under which the builders will have a percentage on work with which they have nothing whatever to do, it seems to me that it is not in line with good business principles.

My hon. friend knows
I was not a member of the committee when the contract was made. I can only state what is known to a great many hon. members, and to the country generally, that when the main contract for the reconstruction of the building was made it was believed- that a large part of the old walls were intact and could be utilized again. I think, however, my hon. friend will admit that the moment it was decided to put the Co-mmdns Chamber in the western end of the building and the Senate in the eastern, it became necessary to tear down a portion of the new work that had been erected in 1907-8. My information is, and I think it is correct, that when the engineers and architects made a critical examination of the building in the spring of 1916 they found they were in error in their first report that practically all the outside walls should be retained, and they decided to tear them down. The architects decided to tear them down. I believe without even the consent of the Minister of Public Works of that , day. I would like to recall to my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) the fact that right up to February of this year the former member for St. John, now the Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick, was a member of that committee. I believe he has had as great an experience in public buildings and public construction as most men in 'Canada, and he heartily concurred in- the decision of the committee. When he has such eminent authority as that, I. do not think he ought to criticise me for at least- following along in his footsteps, believing that whatever was done was done with the best intentions possible.

I distinctly said I was not offering any criticism of my hon. friend [DOT] with regard to his course except at the present time. I recall the hon. gentleman as having taken strong ground that changes might be made in the interest of the country. In so- far as blaming him for following in the footsteps of the former member for St. John is concerned, I may say that that gentleman has gone to a place of safety and he is not responsible to Parliament or to -the people in this matter. If my hon. friend follows in his footsteps he must assume the responsibility U3 well as the honour.

In answer to a question of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) a few days ago, I understood the Minister of Public Works to say that it had been decided not to include quarters' for the Speakers within the new building. Is that correct?
That is correct.

Has any arrangement
been made to provide quarters outside of the building?

No, none whatever. There is a building down in the expropriated area, known as the Manuel hou-se, which the present Speaker has been examining, and it is just possible that it will be fitted up temr porarily for the use of the Speaker until such time as some definite plan can be decided upon. Outside o-f that there have beep no arrangements or even discussions as to what provision will be made for a Speaker s residence in the future.

There used to be frequent references in the press, in the initial stages of this work, to the scope that it was likely to assume, and I recall several very elaborate descriptions of a stack room underground on the face of the cliff or the Lover s Walk. Has that been decided upon as a part of the new building, or has anything definite been done in regard do it?

Nothing has been done about that whatever. I am speaking now without all 'the data before me, but I am sure that no decision has been made, and I do not think it probable that that question will come up in the near future.
Us the exclusion of the Speaker's chamber due to lack of space or to other considerations?

I do not think it is so much for lack of space. There is an enormous amount of space in the new building. I think I am safe in saying that the architects, and a great many people who have investigated it, came to the conclusion that



with the ceilings about 20 feet high an ordinary room would look more like a box turned on its end than a room. It would be an ungainly affair and you would have to have rooms with ceilings such as I have described unless you put the Speaker's quarters up on the third or fourth story. Personally, if I have any feeling in the matter, I would prefer to stick to the old custom of having the Speaker's house within the Parliament buildings. That may be only because I still have some veneration for the antiquities, the records of the past and the- traditions of our fathers. But, after all, we are living in a progressive age, and because Speakers from time immemorial have had their residence in the House of Commons, both in the old country and in this, I do not suggest that we should still follow that custom. I must confess that it is an open question, and' without having any strong feelings one way or the other, I think that in what I am saying I am voicing the sentiments of the gentlemen who were on the Committee and by whom it w>as decided that probably it would be better to forsake the traditions of the past and have the house for modern Speakers either maintained by themselves, or by the country, in some other locality.

I hope I am not lacking in veneration for the older things, but it is not on that- ground alone that quarters should be provided for the Speaker. If it is a matter of principle that the Speaker or any official shall have a residence, there is something to he said in favour of it; and in that case there is an obvious advantage in locating the Speaker's quarters where he can be easily accessible. If the, policy upon the matter has been settled, there is no use in d-iscusising it, but if it is still an open question I certainly favour the idea that the Speaker should have an official residence, and that it should, if possible, be within the Parliament buildings. In the old Parliament buildings the trouble* was, not that the Speaker had a residence, in the building, but that quite a numfber of other people also had residence there, and if they were all to be again included I think the minister would be quite right and that there is no particular reaeon why the. accommodation should not be used for other purposes. So far ae the Speaker of the House is concerned, and I think the remark also applies to the Speaker of the Senate, if they are to have official residence, there is an obvious convenience in having them within the Parliament buildings.
[Mr. CarveltJ

I would like to say that not only should the Speaker be accessible during the session, but as he is charged with the oversight of a great deal of what goes on inside the House, residence on the .spot would be an obvious advantage. Nor does it seem to me that in modern days, when buildings are equipped with elevators and so forth, there is any great objection to putting the Speaker's residence in an upper story. There are, indeed, advantages, to be enjoyed under such circumstances, particularly with such a site ae the one occupied by the Parliament buildings here.
While I am on my feet I would like to support the. remarks of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) when he expressed the hope that we might get into the new House before next session. Despite what the minister has, said, I am inclined to believe that if sufficient effort were made we might be able to occupy and utilize the chambers and sufficient of the new buildings to carry on our work next session. Speaking as a back bencher, who, save when the House is empty, has not the luxury of a front seat, but has to sit on a wooden chair at a very awkward angle, it does not appeal to me that we should be condemned for another session to the present chamber. After all, though Parliament is the place for talk, it has also been well described as a factory for the turning out of the Acts which govern the country, and it strikes me that the plant of this factory is about as inefficient as one could find. Even this evening, and perhaps this is due to my own disability, I had the greatest difficulty in hearing what the Minister of Public Works was saying. He speaks loudly and distinctly, hut in this chamber you often lose a great deal of what is said. I feel quite certain that the poor attendance of members in the House is at times due to these causes of discomfort and bad acoustics. There has been some talk of "ginger groups" in the House. I think if we formed a "ginger group" we might do something towards spurring on the architect with this work. As I understand it, the trouble is not so much with the contractor as with the architect. As the minister has said with regard to the tower, the architect desires to dream for some further days of its beauty. Well, let us finish the interior m some habitable way and let the beauty come later; there will be plenty of time for that. I would still have hope that something may he done to hurry things so

that we might get into the new quarters next session.
Mr. MoCREA: The contractor's commission, I understand, is eight per cent up to four million dollars, and after that seven per cent. What commission or remuneration does the architect receive for his work?
I think it is five and a half per cent.
That probably accounts for his wanting to demolish the whole building.

I have never asked
what animated him, and therefore I am unable to answer the question. I can, however, inform my hon. friend that there are two architects, and between them they receive, I think it is, five and a half per cent commission. They furnish all the technical assistants, with their clerks, and the five and a half per cent covers the total cost to the country of designing and supervising the construction of the building.

I was one of the members who had the extreme pleasure of visiting the new Parliament buildings at the invitation of the Minister of Public Works a few days ago, and I enjoyed the privilege very much. In rambling through the buildings with the Minister of Public Works and the chief architect, the matter of the completion of the Commons and Senate chambers was thoroughly discussed, and I was given to understand in a measure that the completion of the chambers in time for the next session of Parliament was not such an impossibility as seems to have been conveyed to the House to-night, in fact, that it was not altogether impossible. I heartily agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) that, while grumbling at our surroundings may not come with a very good grace from a new member, especially in war times, yet when better conditions could possibly be provided by a little extra effort, that effort should not be lost sight of. I felt confident, from the assurances given me by the Minister of Public Works, that a strong effort would be made towards that end. My own views, on the occasion of our tour through the buildings, did not quite coincide with the ideas of the architect, who was disposed to take all the time possible in completing the structure, and was not disposed to hand over the buildings for occupancy until such time as he had put on the last flourish. THowever, I do not think the
architect's ideas should prevail altogether. I suggested that the workmen should be concentrated from now on upon the completion of the Commons and Senate chambers. If that were done I think there should be no difficulty whatever in having those sections at least finished in time for the next session of Parliament.
The hon. member for London suggested that possibly the .present House would be more comfortable if there were a few more "ginger groups" in it. An hon. gentleman on this side then made the suggestion that we had an exhibition by a "ginger group" not long since, occupying seats almost exactly where the h'on. member for London at present is sitting, which was very much enjoyed by members on both sides, and also, perhaps, by a portion of the gallery. I think where the "ginger" is required is behind the architect. If the committee who have charge of this matter on behalf of the Government, and have the say-so, give the architect distinctly to understand what they want, and insist upon having both chambers finished in proper time, their views would in all probability be carried out.

Reference has been
made to Hon. Mr. Pugsley, the former Minister of Public Works. I did not see very much in that gentleman's record as Minister of Public Works to commend itself to me, but that may have been my fault, not his. We should, however, speak kindly of the absent, as we do of the dead. I am in agreement with the determination arrived at by the Committee to tear down what remained of the walls after the fire. I do not know whether any of these walls could have been utilized, but, though I had no special knowledge of the subject, I thought from the first that it would be a mistake to give the new building an appearance of patch-work by utilizing such walls as were not entirely destroyed. Our country is too big and has too great a future to justify our patching up such an important building as this. With regard to living quarters for the Speakers of the Commons and 'the Senate, I believe that no place should be provided in the building for 'that purpose. I would not provide ciuarters for the Speaker of the Senate, at any rate, because the Senate does not sit very late, and after the Senate rises the Speaker of that House might better be off in a quiet place by himself, resting for the duties Of the next day. Why should we provide, in a building constructed for legislative purposes, living quarters for the

gentleman who happens to be appointed Speaker for three or four years, and is succeeded by somebody else for a similar period? I would give the Speaker only such office quarters as are necessary, where he could be communicated with during office hours by members of the House who desire to see him. Perhaps some hon. gentleman can give me a reason why the Speaker of the Commons or the Speaker of the Senate should be provided with living quarters within the building or a residence outside; for my part I see none. As to our going into the building before next session, it is true that we should all like to do that. The acoustic properties of this Chamber are about as bad as. they possibly can be.
If one happens to be facing the
10	p.m. gentleman who is addressing the House, it is possible to hear what he says, but if you are behind, it is difficult indeed) to hear. While we should all like to get into the new building by next session, it must be remembered that we are spending $5,000,000 in the construction of a home for the future legislators of our country, and we should not proceed with haste. We have had to put up -with inconveniences here for a few sessions, and we can stand them for another session, if necessary. It is not desirable that the construction of the building should be unduly rushed, because as Canadians we all want to see the new building, when it is finished, the finest on the North American continent. It is not a question of a few hundred thousand dollars; the people of Canada are not going to quibble over the cost of this building, which should last for all time. I agree that the. contractors should not make anything out of such things as pictures and decorations-I am glad to have the minister's assurance in that regard-but there should be no cheese-paring in the matter of the cost of the building. We want to make it as fine as architectural genius can make it; we want it to he something which may be pointed to with pride by the people of our own country and looked upon by others who come here as something worthy of this great country and its future.

With the member for
Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) I am in complete agreement as to the disappearance of the Speaker's residence from the Parliament building. I see no reason for an official residence for the Speaker within the building. The reasons advanced by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mir. Fielding) that the Speaker should be at all times

accessible does not entail the placing of an official residence within the walls of the Parliament 'building. So long as the Speaker has an office there, like any other official of Parliament, and. is accessible ' within office hours, that meets all the requirements of Parliament. The very presence of these quarters in the old building led to certain features that nobody would associate with legislation-some of which, I think, the member for Shelburne and Queen's had in mind when he made his brief remarks. For that reason, I hope that the present decision. to keep the building free of an official residence for the Speaker of either House will be adhered to. I need not add anything to the suggestion made to the minister as to the general desire that exists for completing the building. At the same time, that advice must be qualified, as the member for Frontenaic has said; we must not rush the construction of the building at the expense of its excellence. That, I am sure, is not in the mind of any hon. gentleman who has spoken this evening.

Would it be possible to have work on the chamber proceed to the extent that we could occupy it during the session, and to suspend the work on the building while the House was sitting? Of course, we are all anxious to get into the new building in order that we may have more comfortable quarters, but to rush the completion of the chamber itself might be detrimental to the rest of the building. At the same time, it would not be desirable for us to deliberate while the noise of hammers and saws was being heard around us. I think that we should go on with the work gradually, so that when we occupy the building we shall be not only comfortable, hut quiet as well. As to the quarters for the Speaker, I agree with the member for Frontenac. It is not often that we meet on the same ground and shake hands, but tonight it happens that we entertain the same opinion. I do not believe that the Speaker of either House ought to have living quarters within the building. As long as they are where we can reach them, the purposes of Parliament can be served; if the Speaker has an office in the building that is all we want. He may live in any part of the city, and proceed to and from the House by motor car or other means of transportation; so that it would not be any disadvantage to members if he lived outside.
Tramway.

We may require him after the street cars stop running. It would be better for the country to pay for a motor car to be used by the Speaker than to establish quarters for him within the Parliament building.
When my hon. friend speaks about the noise of saws and hammers around the House of Commons, does he include the Senate?

I am glad we have had this discussion, and I would not have objected 'had every member of the Committee to-night expressed his views, upon these matters, because the Government as such is taking practically no responsibility over the erection of this building. We look upon this as the home for the future Parliament of Canada, and, as such, jit 'is being constructed by, the Committee of the Parliament of Canada, acting, of course, under the advice, to a very great extent, of the technical gentlemen who have been employed to assist it. The very fact that there has been such a difference of opinion expressed here to-night as to whether we should hurry on the work so as to occupy the building next year, and whether we should have the Speaker's quarters within or without the building, or anywhere at all, shows (that the committee 'have some difficulty in deciding upon these very important questions. I have no objection whatever (to the "ginger group" to which my hon. friend refers, in discussing the matter from every angle, and I would not care if there was a " dynamite group."
Have them on the lawn.

So far as the construction of this Parliament building is concerned, I would be glad to hear all the criticisms and all the suggestions which any hon. member can offer, because I realize this is not a contentious matter. It is purely a matter of getting the very finest building which we can get consistently with the reasonable amount of money at our disposal. But I am very much impressed by the suggestion made by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). He is usually pretty logical when 'he wants to be.
When he wants to be? That is a modification.

My hon. friend suggests that it will be pretty hard to hold a session of Parliament with a hundred workmen working all around us finishing up the remainder of the building-for I do not believe it would be possible before next session
to do more than finish up those 84 rooms, the two chambers and some of the corridors. There would have to be an army of workmen working in and around the buildipg while the House was in session. There are other things hon. members are forgetting. This would give no accommodation for the working staff of the House. We must have accommodation for the officials of the House. If my hon. friends can devise any scheme whatever whereby they can hurry up the architect, or the contractor, or the committee, or any other person or body of persons having jurisdiction or power, I shall be very glad to carry it out. But it would not be good business to hurry up the completion of the building at the expense of efficiency.	.

As to responsibility m the matter, I would draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that the contract is not made with the committee. The contract is between the Department of Public Works and the contractor. The contract was executed by the Minister of Public Works who represents His Majesty, the King, and the contractor, not by the committee.	,
I presume that is true because the committee would have no legal standing.

I just wish to endorse what has been said by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) with regard to the Speaker's quarters, and also with regard to hurrying up the erection of the building to the neglect of the work. Most of us are anxious to get into the new building-I am not particularly worrying about it; I can sit here as well as anybody, although the new building would be much more comfortable than this one- but I would not like to see the work neglected on account of too much haste.

Any one who has seen the stage to which the new building has been carried will admit that it is practically physically impossible to4 complete it in time for the next session of Parliament. I would just like to make one' suggestion. I agree with all that has been said about the discomforts of this chamber. As a new member, possibly I should not pass my opinion, but it is quite true this chamber is not what it ought to be, and the suggestion I wish to make is this: that the authorities ought to endeavour to make it as comfortable as possible for the next session. if we do have to spend next session

here. Perhaps one of the greatest difficulties with which we have to contend is in the matter of acoustics-we cannot understand.the members as they speak. That difficulty can very largely be overcome if every hon. member who rises to speak attempts to speak a3 distinctly as possible, and I believe we ourselves can overcome most of the difficulties in that direction for one session at least. I would like to express the opinion that, when the seating arrangements of this Chamber were made, they seemed to be made with the one distinct idea of making them as uncomfortable as possible. I am referring to the chairs and the seating arrangements, and the matter of heating and ventilation. Many of us have perhaps acquired the first colds of this winter since coming into this House. It is quite possible, with a Little care, to make the accommodation here a good deal better than it has been.

The fire alarm system in this building indicates by lights on what story a fire occurs. Should a fire start on the second story, a light of a certain colour will appear showing where the fire is. Is that the system' to be adopted in the new building, or is the old system to be used?

I could not answer that question; in fact I do not think the matter has been discussed. The system installed in this building is certainly a very excellent-one. It was installed by a gentleman who is employed on the staff, in fact, who has charge of this building. By pressing a button, it indicates by a light which floor the fire is on, and whether it be to the right or to the left of the main entrance. It shows the stand pipe and it is certainly a wonderful contrivance. As regards the new building the matter has not been discussed-, but it woVld certainly be worthy of discussion.

The'new building will
be fireproof?
Yes, and I cannot conceive there will ever be a fire in the new building. That may be a violent assumption.

The Titanic " could not
be sunk."

This is stronger even
than the Titanic. There will not be a particle of wood of any kind or description in this new building excepting the doors, iand, I think, base boards around the inside of the offices. There are no door frames as such; there are no wooden win-
dow frames or wooden sashes; everything is either metal or concrete. Therefore, while you might burn the desks and papers in a room, while you might possibly conceive of snch a condition of affairs that would burn the doors, that would be the end of it, 6o that I am not bothering my head very .much about a fire alarm in the new building-	.
Ottawa eastern departmental block-new fireproof roof, eta, 1120,000.

This item has been carried along for a number of years, and it is very doubtful if any money will be expended during the coming year. In peace times it would be proper to expend this money, not so much to make the East Block waterproof beoause it is that very well now, but to make it fireproof especially that portion of the building'occupied by the Finance and Treasury Departments. They have fairly safe vaults. Money is scarce, and the roof will have to be in a good deal worse state than it is now before we shall spend any money on it this year.
Ottawa-new public building:, $1,0-00,000.

What has the minister in contemplation?
Air. CARVELiL: When I assumed the duties of Minister of Public Works, pretty nearly every morning a request was laid on my desk for more space, and the officers of the department were spending a good deal of their time hunting around the city seeing where it was- possible to house the Service. The Service, of course, has grown very much of late and necessarily so; .the war has brought -additional responsibilities, and adequate quarters must be provided for the officials. I asked the deputy to furnish me at once with a statement- of the number of buildings, their location and description, rented by the Government in t'he city of Ottawa. I have not the list here, but I can tell the committee in a general way that when this statement was made up some two months ago we were paying rentals in the city of Ottawa amounting to $657,000 a year. To be absolutely accurate, I should say that some portion of that coveis heating and elevator service paid for by the landlords-, but after making every reasonable deduction, I think I*am safe in saying that the actual rentals paid by the Government in the city of Ottawa amount to $600,000 a year, and they run all the way from 40 cents to $1 and $1.25 a square foot-I know of one case where it is even more than that. There seems to be no plan or

system upon which one can. go. It is a question to some extent of location. Those new buildings on Sparks street, for instance, naturally command a higher rental than older buildings. But the Government has been driven to the point where it is not a question of getting the beat building on Sparks street, but of going wherever the space can be had and paying almost what the landlords like to charge; we are about in the position that we have not anything to say about it. Now it was proposed by the officers of the department that we should erect a building on the block between Albert and Queen streets, on the west side of O'Connor street. That, of course, raised a question which has been discussed in the newspapers to a great extent, and I am finding no fault with that, because that is w'hat newspapers are for; every member of the community has a perfect right to go to the newspapers and discuss matters pertaining to the public welfare. Some three or four years ago a commission was appointed to prepare and lay before the Government a general plan for the construction and development of governmental offices. That plan is now in our possession, and while I am not sufficient of a landscape artist to pass judgment upon it, it looks all right to me. But if we erected to-day a building in keeping with that plan, north of Wellington street, either west of the old Supreme Court buildings or on Sussex street, it would necessitate a pretty high type of building because I do not think the people of Canada would want those in authority to erect permanent office buildings on a grand scale unless they were built in keeping with the general architectural design submitted to the Government. I think I am safe in saying that if will cost 75 per cent more to erect a building to-day than it did four or five years ago or than it will cost probably four or five years hence. The question of time is also a very important element, I could not bring myself to believe that I should be justified as a business man in starting on the erection of a building in keeping with that general plan. We should be spending a very large amount of money for the space we obtained, and should also be losing a lot of valuable time, because we could not possibly have any one unit of a building ot that class ready for occupation inside of two or three years. We therefore got the officers of the department to figure on an ordinary office building on the site which I have mentioned. I thought I expressed my wishes in fairly dear language; I think I have the faculty of making people understand what I mean as a rule, and I certainly wanted nothing but a real, good, substantial business block erected. The site we decided upon is 200 feet square, and we proposed to erect a building 200 feet long by 150 feet wide, with an opening in the centre 100 feet by 50 feet; that would give a corridor around the whole building, which was to be nine stories high, and every room would have light and air on one side. We asked the 'Chief Architect to make an estimate, and in the month of January he estimated that a building of this size containing 700 rooms and 140,000 square feet of floor space could be erected for $1,076,250. We estimated that the site would cost $200,000; so the building would cost altogether about one and a half million dollars. I took the'matter up with Council, where it was discussed and decided upon as a matter of policy. Specifications were prepared and we called for tenders, but before the tenders were in for the main building it was thought^and I am satisfied we were correct-that we could do better by calling for tenders for the steel work ourselves, making a separate contract for that work. We received a tender from the Dominion Bridge Company for $334,000, and one from the Hamilton Bridge Works for $358,000. The architect's estimate was $325,000. We therefore accepted the tender of the Dominion Bridge Company, the lowest tender. When the tenders were received for the main building, by adding to that the tender we had received from the Dominion Bridge Company, we found that the building was going to cost -I do not want to give the exact figures here because it might affect future tenders -some four or five hundred thousand dollars more than we had been told it would cost. When those tenders were brought to me I naturally asked some questions, and going over the specifications. I found that we were building a work of art instead of a business building. I found copper roofs, copper doors, marble slabs, in fact everything which a man could imagine from an artistic standpoint. But I did not find it very much better from a business standpoint, and therefore I gave instructions to cut things down and see what could be done. They are working at it now and producing wonderful results. The new plans will be ready for inspection probably within the next day or two, and if we can succeed in having this building erected on a purely business basis and for a reasonable figure, we are going to do it; if we cannot, we shall have to resort to some other expedient. either.

somewhat of a New Brunswick name.

Can the minister tell me
whether the price of the land is included in this vote or the amounts previously spent?

I can only say that the price of the land is included in the amount

*
previously given, but what that amount was I am not in a position to state at the present time. I think it is very important that the work should be proceeded with as soon as possible, because I was told yesterday by Mr. Davy, who happened to be in Ottawa, that the partial blowing-up of the Halifax dry dock would 'bring a lot of ship repairing business to Quebec ini fact, that the shipyards of Quebec and Montreal would have to look after mostly all the business of ship repairing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

I hope that my hon.
friend, or any other members' of the House-either, will not get the idea that the Halifax dry dock is out of commission. That dock was put out of commission by the explosion which occurred last winter, and I may as well state here, and I am. glad to-have the opportunity of doing so, that the Minister of Railways and Canals and myself spent three or four days- in the city of Halifax after the explosion. At that time there were eight or nine ships in the harbour which would have to enter the dry dock, and we -at once entered into negotiations with the owners, the dry dock being a private institution. The owners claimed that they were unable to finish the dock, and would not finish it. They wanted us to buy it, which we did not feel like doing, and we started in to make repairs. The owners are to pay towards the cost the amount of their insurance, which is 111,000, and we are putting up the balance, an amount which will not be very great.
However, the first thing was to get, this dock in commission, and it has been in commission for nearly two months. The ship that was in. it was repaired and sent out, and I believe that another has since been taken in, repaired and sent out. The Halifax dry dock, therefore, is operating just as it was a year ago. But that does not obviate the necessity of placing the Champlain dry dock in commission at the earliest possible moment; in fact, it could be operated almost immediately. This dock is in two compartments: there is a gate in the centre which can he closed so that one end may be used as a dry dock and the other to contain water, or vice versa. The outer section could be, and, I imagine,

is,	being used to-day. In addition to that, we have the old dry dock, which has ansvyered the purposes of the St. Lawrence during the last twenty or twenty-five years. I can assure my hon. friends that the work will be pushed forward as rapidly as possible, and will be entirely completed within a few months.
I ishould like to know what the policy of the Government is in the matter of building dry docks. Do we own a dry dock at Esquimalt?
Yes, and one at Kingston .
The dry dock at Esquimalt was passed over from the Imperial Government to the Dominion.
Yes.
I am not aware that the Government owns any dry docks on the Atlantic coast.

No. The Government has no particular policy with regard to the construction of dry docks except that which is embodied in the Dry Dock Subsidies Act, which was passed in 1908 or 1909 and subsequently amended. The dimensions of a first-class dry dock have been increased to 1,150 feet in length, and a guarantee of interest is provided at 41 per cent for a period of thirty-five years on an amount not exceeding $4,500,000.

Attempts have been made by different Ministers of Public Works to make the Dry Dock Subsidies Act more attractive than it was .at the beginning, but so far no business concern has taken advantage of its .provisions. If the Government are going into the business of build-dry docks, private companies 11 p.m. will not fake advantage of this Act, [because they would then come into competition with the Government. I suppose there is not much use in suggesting any large public expenditure just now, but I wish to point out that the harbour of Sydney, with its proximity to Newfoundland and its importance in connection with trans-Atlantic traffic, is becoming a great shipping and commercial centre. But, excepting a marine railway, no facilities have been provided there to take care of ships. I understand that the matter has been discussed in the other House by Senator McLennan, who comes from practically the same place that I do. I should like the enterprising Minister of Public Works to take into consideration the
fact that we have great need for a dry dock in that part of the country, particularly in view of the presence there of large steel works; and I hope that he will remember this, if the policy of building dry docks is to be carried out by the Government.

I appreciate everything my hon. friend has said about the harbour of Sydney. It is certainly a very beautiful sheet of water, especially in summer, and I hope that some enterprising citizen or citizens in that part of Nova Scotia will come forward with a business proposal under the Dry Dock Subsidies Act. If they do, I assure him, they will receive every encouragement that the department can give them. The same applies to similar proposals which might be made in other parts of the country. A floating dry dock has been built under the Dry Dock Subsidies Act by the Vickers people in Montreal.
That was imported from the Old Country?

Yes. Another floating dock which was brought from the Old Country, has been built at Prince Rupert under the Dry Dock Subsidies Act. I think these are the only two which have been built under that Act. However, the Act is there, and it is open 'to any body of capitalists who wish to invest some of their own money -in these public enterprises to take advantage of its provisions. I should like to inculcate a spirit of giving into some of the capitalists of Canada. I have watched them very carefully during the last fourteen or fifteen years, and I have observed on their part a great willingness to receive public money; I hope that I can now cause them to realize the importance of the duty of giving money to the public. I should like to see these gentlemen put up some of their own money to build these works, accept Government subsidies, and become real patriots. By doing this they would build up a better public sentiment than we have in Canada at present. I do not say that the Government will or will not adopt any particular policy with regard to the construction of these docks, but I throw out the suggestion to many capitalists who have grown wealthy during the last three or four years, that they come along with a real business proposal for the construction of dry docks in the large centres of Canada.

The Vickers people
have been very enterprising. I happen to know that firm- because their works are

located in my new constituency of Maison-neuve. Although they had invested a large amount of money, for many years they did little work. Since the war began, however, they have been fortunate, and at the same time they have rendered valuable service to the British Admiralty. During the first year of the war I saw there two or three cruisers which had taken part in the famous naval engagement off the Falkland Islands. The Vickers have been growing and developing, and I daresay they have , to-day one of the largest shipyards on the North American continent.
They come within the class of men whom I should like to see doing business in this line.

May I call attention to the danger which exists of our crippling the shipyards of Canada if we apply not only the spirit but the letter of the new Order in Council concerning conscription to employees of ship-building establishments? Conscription is the law, it is true, and must be obeyed. But I was speaking yesterday to a prominent shipbuilder who was at a loss to understand how the Government could deprive his shipyard of from one hundred to two hundred of his hands-riveters, heaters, riggers, shipwrights, plumbers, furnace men, boilermakers, draughtsmen.
Although it seems rather easy for any one to become a heater or a riveter, yet this shipbuilder was explaining to me that it took not months merely, but several years of training for a man to become a good heater or a good riveter. I beg to draw the attention of the Government to the necessity of protecting, I shall not say the shipbuilding of the country, but the shiprepairing that will take place during the months to come. I was just mentioning the case of one or two cruisers which took part in the engagement at the Falkland Islands and which were repaired at Vickers during the first year of the war. Since then, this has not been made public, but the Vickers Company in Montreal and the Davy Company in Quebec have done a quantity of work for the Imperial Government; they have built submarines, destroyers, chasers and trawlers. They have contracts with the Imperial Government, the Dominion Government and the governments of the Allied countries. They have cancelled some contracts which they had with neutral govern-meats. We should treat this question as business men and see to it that this industry

is not crippled at this very crucial moment of the war.

I quite appreciate what my hon. friend states. I realize the importance of those shipyards, as I had the pleasure of going through them in December last. I was very much impressed with the evidence of business which I saw there. I shall be glad to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and the Minister of Militia and Defence to the statement made by my hon. friend this evening.

Speaking roughly, about 83,400,000.

This amount of money is very well spent. For years past, I remember, the shipping interests have made every effort with the Government to secure a dry dock to accommodate big ships, should an accident occur. Will the minister express his opinion as to the possibility of utilizing such a nice harbour as Quebec harbour as a free port?

I am afraid my hon. friend is asking me to answer something which I would not feel in a position to answer. I have not given the matter any study. Possibly at some future time I might give him a more studied opinion upon it.
